jdso8u-d1e167-d1e108.summary: Title (Wadding q.4) and first argument against theology being practical: John 20 says these things were written that you may believe; believing is speculative, since vision succeeds it.
claims: Scripture is written so that we may believe.
Belief is speculative, as vision succeeds it.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e132.summary: Second argument: practical knowledge concerns the contingent (De anima III, Ethics I), but this science's object is necessary, not contingent.
claims: Practical knowledge concerns contingents.
Theology's object is necessary.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e160.summary: Third argument: Boethius (De Trinitate) names theology as one of three speculative sciences, and he seems to mean this theology, since he says its subject is the first substance, the substance of God that lacks matter.
claims: Boethius classes theology, about immaterial divine substance, as speculative.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e185.summary: Fourth argument: some speculative science is nobler than any practical science, yet none is nobler than this one, so it is speculative. Speculative science is nobler because it is for its own sake while practical science is for use, and because it is more certain (Metaphysics I).
claims: Speculative science is nobler than practical, being for its own sake and more certain.
No science is nobler than theology.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e206.summary: Fifth argument, parallel to Aristotle's for metaphysics (Metaphysics I): this science was sought once all necessities were secured, to escape ignorance, since care for necessities impedes inquiry into it; so it is speculative.
claims: A science pursued after necessities, to escape ignorance, is speculative.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e228.summary: Arguments for the opposite: the end of the law is love (Romans 13 [1 Tim 1:5]); the whole law and prophets hang on the two commandments (Matthew 22); Augustine says whoever keeps charity in conduct holds all that is hidden and open in the divine words. These show theology is not merely for contemplation, whereas a speculative science requires nothing beyond contemplation (Avicenna).
claims: The end of the law is charity.
Theology is not solely for contemplation, so it is not purely speculative.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e280.summary: Second question: whether a science is called practical per se from its ordering to praxis as its end. For: De anima III says the intellect becomes practical by extension and differs from speculative intellect by its end.
claims: Practical and speculative intellect differ by their ends (De anima III).

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e304.summary: Further: Metaphysics I says practical science is less noble than speculative because it is for use, which holds only if use is the per se end of that habit.
claims: Practical science is less noble because its per se end is use.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e326.summary: Further: Metaphysics II says the end of speculative science is truth, of practical science, work.
claims: Speculative science aims at truth, practical at work.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e341.summary: Against: Aristotle distinguishes practical from speculative sciences by objects, not ends (Metaphysics VI, for active and productive sciences; Ethics VI, distinguishing the calculative from the scientific by contingent and necessary objects; De anima III, assigning the practical intellect the good that is doable and contingent). So a science is practical per se by its object, not by praxis as end.
claims: Aristotle distinguishes practical and speculative sciences by their objects.
The practical intellect's object is the doable, contingent good.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e388.summary: Scotus starts from a general point all concede: a practical habit somehow extends to praxis. He will examine first what praxis is, second how practical knowledge extends to it, third from what knowledge has this extension.
claims: A practical habit extends to praxis in some way.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e418.summary: First article: praxis is an act of a power other than the intellect, naturally posterior to intellection, apt to be elicited in conformity with right reason in order to be right. The first condition holds because within intellectual acts there is no extension beyond the intellect. If one intellectual act directs another, the second is not praxis and the first not practical knowledge, else logic, which directs reasoning, would be practical.
claims: Praxis is an act of a non-intellectual power, naturally posterior to intellection, apt to conform to right reason.
One intellectual act directing another does not make it practical; otherwise logic would be practical.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e468.summary: The second condition: acts not ordered to intellect (vegetative acts) or naturally preceding intellection (sensory acts, and sensory appetite as preceding intellect, common to us and animals) are not praxis, and practical knowledge does not extend to them as prior. It concerns them only insofar as it moderates them and they follow the moderating intellection.
claims: Vegetative and pre-intellectual sensory acts are not praxis.
Practical knowledge bears on such acts only as moderating them.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e514.summary: Corollary: praxis is only an act of will, elicited or commanded, since no other act is essentially posterior to intellection; for any other act, one of the same kind could occur before intellection, as a survey of the other powers shows.
claims: Praxis is only an elicited or commanded act of will.
Only acts of will are essentially posterior to intellection.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e547.summary: Second proof: praxis is an act in the knower's power. Ethics VI shows the craftsman needs art to act rightly and needs no virtue for what is not in his power, so his making is in his power, and the prudent man's virtuous action even more. Since only elicited or commanded acts of will are in our power, praxis is such an act.
claims: Praxis is in the agent's power.
Only acts elicited or commanded by the will are in our power.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e596.summary: Objection: then some intellection would be praxis, since an intellection can be commanded by the will like acts of other powers; so the first condition (praxis belongs to a power other than intellect) is false.
claims: Intellections commanded by the will would count as praxis.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e623.summary: Reply: speculation is a kind of operation and so, extending the term, praxis; but taking praxis strictly, as only the operation to which intellect can extend, no intellection is praxis, and this is the sense when practical knowledge is said to extend to praxis.
claims: In the strict sense, no intellection is praxis.
concepts: strict and broad sense of praxis

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e643.summary: So 'an intellection is commanded by the will, therefore it is praxis' does not follow; what follows is that it is praxis or practical, being denominated quasi-accidentally from the praxis it can extend to, not being its term. Conversely, every praxis is an elicited or commanded act of will; inferring the denial of the first condition from the second commits the fallacy of the consequent.
claims: A commanded intellection is denominated practical but is not the term of practical extension.
Inferring that intellection is praxis from its being commanded commits the fallacy of the consequent.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e678.summary: The third condition: Ethics VI says right choice requires right reason, which holds of every right volition, since it must be elicited in conformity with right reason; every praxis is a volition or follows one, so every praxis is apt to be elicited conformably with right reason. Also, per Augustine (De Trinitate XV), the intellect understands for itself and others, so it can judge acts of other powers before they are elicited, and if it judges rightly they must conform to it to be right.
claims: Every right volition requires conformity with right reason.
The intellect can judge acts of other powers before they are elicited.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e740.summary: From the last two conditions: an act commanded by the will is not primarily praxis but quasi-accidentally, since it is neither primarily posterior to intellection nor primarily apt to conform with right reason; it has these through the volition. So praxis is primarily the elicited act of will.
claims: Commanded acts are praxis only derivatively.
Primarily, praxis is the elicited act of the will.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e773.summary: Further: whatever is primarily such when joined to something posterior would still be such if separated. The will's act can be separated from acts of other powers wherever the will can act but lower powers cannot, as with all immaterial objects; so about all such objects there is an act of will, and it alone is praxis.
claims: The will's act is praxis even when no act of another power follows.
Concerning immaterial objects, only the will's act can be praxis.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e815.summary: Second proof from De anima III: Aristotle concludes there are two movers, appetite and reason, says intellect does not move without appetite, that will is appetite, and that appetites can be contrary, so the moving principle is one in species (appetite). As sensory appetite with sense and imagination is a moving principle, so will with intellect and reason. So as an act of sensory appetite following cognition is true praxis without any outward transition, so is an act of will, even alone without a commanded act, and even when opposed by sensory appetite.
claims: Will, with intellect, is a moving principle as sensory appetite is with sense.
An act of will following intellection is true praxis even without outward action.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e899.summary: Second article: the extension of practical knowledge to praxis consists in two aptitudinal relations, conformity and natural priority. Priority comes from Ethics VI as cited; conformity from the same place, where practical truth is truth in agreement with right appetite.
claims: Practical extension consists in aptitudinal relations of natural priority and conformity to praxis.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e931.summary: The relations are aptitudinal, not actual: that a conforming praxis actually follows is wholly accidental and contingent to the consideration. If knowledge were practical by actual extension, none would be necessarily practical, but the same knowledge would be now practical and now speculative, which is absurd.
claims: Practical knowledge is practical by aptitude, not by actual extension.
Otherwise the same knowledge would shift between practical and speculative.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e966.summary: Clarification: practical knowledge is commonly said to extend to praxis as directive to directed or rule to ruled. Being naturally prior and conformable means not being conformed to praxis as prior but being that to which praxis is to be conformed, i.e. directing and regulating praxis. Whether such directing involves efficient causality is treated in II d.25.
claims: Practical knowledge directs praxis as a rule to which it should conform.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1005.summary: It follows that practical and speculative are not essential differences of knowledge in general, which is something absolute: practical names a twofold aptitudinal relation to praxis, speculative the privation of that relation, and neither belongs to the essence of an absolute. It is like dividing a genus by properties of species, as number into even and odd or line into straight and curved; practicality or speculativity belongs to some knowledge per se in the second mode, from a cause intrinsic to the subject.
claims: Practical and speculative are not essential differences of knowledge.
They are like properties dividing a genus, belonging per se in the second mode.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1056.summary: Third article, from what knowledge has this extension. One opinion (Henry of Ghent's): intellect is called practical from one thing, habit or act from another. Habits and acts are practical because they concern the operable true, a formally distinct special object. The intellect is practical only when it orders what it apprehends to work, which happens only when moved by appetite for the end; so the practical intellect connotes a necessary ordering to explicit desire of the end and implicit desire of the means.
claims: On this view, habits and acts are practical by their object, the operable true.
The intellect is practical only when moved by desire for the end to order its knowledge to work.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1111.summary: Continuing that opinion: since being ordered to work is accidental to the speculable, though being orderable is not, the difference between speculative and practical intellect is accidental and through relation to something outside the intellect, while the difference of habits and acts is formal, by the formal difference between operable and non-operable objects. So De anima III says they differ by end, and Ethics VI that the good of practical intellect is truth agreeing with right appetite.
claims: On this view, practical and speculative intellect differ accidentally, by end.
Practical and speculative habits differ formally, by object.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1156.summary: The opinion's example: speculative intellect apprehends health as a fitting good; appetite desires it and somewhat follows practical counsel that health should be acquired. With desire of the end in place, the practical intellect reasons from the principle that what best attains it should be procured, ending in the final conclusion of counsel. The whole reasoning takes its start from the apprehended desired end, the first object of practical intellect, and aims at acting on its findings, so it presupposes willing the end and is ordered to the choice that follows counsel.
claims: Practical reasoning starts from the desired end and ends in counsel ordered to choice.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1202.summary: Summary and first objection: the opinion distinguishes practical and speculative intellect by an end accidental to the object, but habits by formal differences of objects. Against: Metaphysics II says of habits that the end of speculative science is truth and of practical, work.
claims: Aristotle distinguishes the habits themselves by end.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1237.summary: Second objection: then a practical habit could be in the speculative intellect without making it practical, which seems absurd, since the possessor is denominated from a habit according to its nature.
claims: A subject is denominated by its habit's nature, so a practical habit should make the intellect practical.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1255.summary: The opinion's reply to the first objection: the end of practical science is work in potency and aptitude, insofar as its object is operable per se; but the operable object is considered by that habit universally, which does not suffice to submit it to actual particular operation. Since act is better than potency in goods, a particular actual consideration is required, which comes from another habit than practical science, found only in the practical intellect.
claims: Practical science aims at work only aptitudinally and universally.
A further habit, in the practical intellect, gives particular actual consideration.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1295.summary: The opinion's reply to the second objection: the intellect can be called practical denominatively from the habit, not simply but in a qualified sense.
claims: The intellect is practical from its habit only in a qualified sense.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1308.summary: Against: then a practical habit and act could be in the speculative intellect, since something practical by nature can exist in the intellect without the posited relation to an act of will. The opinion would grant this but posit another habit in the practical intellect, generated not just from practical acts but from acts of the practical intellect.
claims: The opinion must allow practical habits in the speculative intellect and posit a further habit in the practical intellect.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1339.summary: Against: a practical habit generated from practical acts would suffice for whatever the habit generated from acts of the practical intellect would direct, since the will's commanding the consideration for an end gives the consideration no further directive ratio, nor the habit generated from it.
claims: The will's ordering adds no directive content, so the second habit is superfluous.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1365.summary: Further: many accidents of the same species would then be in the same subject, since the will's ordering or not cannot make acts or habits specifically distinct.
claims: The will's ordering cannot specifically distinguish acts or habits.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1383.summary: Third, against the opinion itself: a subject is denominated more from a per se, essential condition of its accident than an accidental one. If the intellect can be called practical from an accidental condition of its habit (the will's ordering), much more from the essential ordering by which the act is essentially practical. So intellect, habit and act seem called practical from the same thing, though accidentally for the intellect.
claims: Intellect, habit and act are practical from the same source.
Denomination from essential conditions has priority over accidental ones.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1430.summary: A second opinion: habits and acts are called practical from the end, the extension of practical knowledge to praxis, which is extension to the end. The authorities cited earlier support it.
claims: On this view, practicality comes from the end.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1449.summary: Argument for the second opinion: a habit is practical either from object or from end. Not from object, since the intellect becomes practical by extension, which is true only of the same intellect first speculative and then practical when extended to work; so practical and speculative consideration can concern the same object.
claims: Practical and speculative consideration can concern the same object.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1482.summary: Second argument: medicine is divided into speculative and practical, yet both concern the same subject, health or the curable body.
claims: Speculative and practical medicine share a subject.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1498.summary: Third argument: an act is practical because morally good or bad; moral goodness and badness come from circumstances, chief among which is the end.
claims: Moral goodness comes from circumstances, chiefly the end.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1516.summary: Against the second opinion: are habits practical from actual or aptitudinal extension to work? Not actual, as shown and conceded, or an idle craftsman would lack practical knowledge. So aptitudinal; but an aptitude belongs to one nature and not another only because of something absolute in it, so the consideration has an intrinsic condition grounding it. This comes from a prior cause, intellect or object; not intellect, or all considerations would be practical; so from the object.
claims: Practicality is aptitudinal, and aptitude presupposes an intrinsic absolute condition.
That condition must come from the object, not the intellect.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1591.summary: If one says the end is a prior cause, indeed first (Avicenna), and could ground this aptitude: the end causes only as loved and desired, moving the agent; but the aptitude belongs to the consideration whether or not the end is loved, whatever the will's state, even if no will were joined to the intellect. So it does not come from the end as final cause, since nothing has from a cause what it has without that cause causing.
claims: The end causes only as actually loved.
Practical aptitude exists regardless of the will's love, so it does not come from the end.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1640.summary: If one says the end is apt to be loved before the aptitude exists in the knowledge: this does not help, since an effect has nothing from a cause apt to cause unless it actually causes; and the end actually causes as final cause only when actually loved and moving the agent.
claims: An effect receives nothing from a merely potential cause.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1673.summary: Further: the end makes a habit practical either as elicited and possessed outside, as considered, or as intended. Not as elicited, since then it is posterior to the habit and an effect, which does not distinguish its cause. If as known, it has the ratio of object, so the object distinguishes. If as intended, this has been refuted, since such knowledge exists naturally before it is intended.
claims: The end makes knowledge practical only insofar as it is known, i.e. as object.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1710.summary: Further: if being practical and being ordered to praxis as end were convertible, moral science would not be practical, contrary to Aristotle (Ethics I and X), since its end is happiness, which consists in contemplation, not praxis (Ethics X).
claims: Moral science's end is happiness, which is contemplation.
So defining practicality by end would make moral science non-practical.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1739.summary: If one says happiness is the remote end and praxis (directing to virtuous action) the proximate end: directing is necessarily ordered only aptitudinally, so moral science would be practical because it is apt to direct, i.e. directive; but directive and practical are the same (second article), so it is practical because practical, which is empty. Also directing is an act of the intellect, elicited from prudence, and no intellectual act is praxis (first article).
claims: Saying moral science is practical because ordered to directing is circular.
Directing is an intellectual act and so not praxis.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1791.summary: Another response: the end of moral science, as of prudence, is the act of moral virtue to which it is ordered, and that act is praxis.
claims: The end of moral science is the act of moral virtue, which is praxis.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1807.summary: Against: not every practical knowledge has praxis as its end, for some practical intellection concerns the praxis of lower powers (sensory appetite, motive power). No act of a lower power is the end of an intellectual act, since the less noble is not per se the end of the nobler, and intellection is nobler than any act of a lower sensory power.
claims: The less noble cannot be the per se end of the nobler.
Intellection is nobler than acts of lower powers.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1845.summary: Reply offered: although intellection is nobler in the order of nature than an operation of a lower power, it is not so in the moral order, for it is morally better to act bravely than to think about acting bravely.
claims: In the moral order, acting bravely is better than thinking of acting bravely.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1863.summary: Against this, first: it assumes something false. A lower power's act is morally good only by conforming to right reason as its rule, so the rectitude of reason causes the goodness of the act, not conversely; for reason's act to be such a rule is for it to be morally good. Confirmation: prudence is simply nobler than moral virtue in the sensory appetite, so its act is better, and as practical it is better than the other as practical or morally good.
claims: Lower acts are morally good only by conformity to right reason.
Reason's act as rule is itself morally good.
Prudence is nobler than moral virtue in sensory appetite.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1909.summary: Hence the argument from thinking about acting bravely fails: comparing excellence one should compare best to best. The counterpart of acting bravely is the intellect's dictating, according to prudence, to act bravely, and this is morally better, since as rule it has formal moral goodness (its proper rectitude), while the other is only materially good, not morally good of itself apart from its ordering to the rule and to the commanding will.
claims: Excellence should be compared best to best.
The prudential dictate has formal moral goodness; the external act only material goodness.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e1957.summary: Second: the reply is beside the point. The question is from what an intellection is practical, without presupposing that it is practical, since its first circumstance (the end) is being investigated. So intellection is taken only in natural being; distinguishing moral and natural goodness presupposes what is sought.
claims: Appealing to moral goodness presupposes the practicality under investigation.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2001.summary: Others correct the opinion: a habit is called practical from its end, which is practical consideration, since a habit's proper end is its act. Against: if that consideration is practical, it has a cause from which it is so, either its end, already refuted, or its object; then the object is the prior cause from which both habit (mediately) and act are called practical, which is Scotus's point.
claims: If a habit is practical from its act, the act's practicality must come from its object.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2054.summary: Scotus concedes that a habit is not primarily practical from its own act, which is practical from a prior cause, and that no knowledge is per se practical because ordered to praxis as end. Yet it can sometimes have its first extension, conformity to praxis, from the end of the praxis, not as end but as first object.
claims: Knowledge is not practical because ordered to praxis as end.
The end of a praxis can ground practicality as first object, not as end.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2094.summary: First point: practical first principles are sometimes taken from the end of praxis, and then that end, as first cause in this genus, virtually contains the whole knowledge, which has its quiddity and aptitude from it.
claims: When practical principles are drawn from the end, the end virtually contains the practical knowledge.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2114.summary: Second point: the end of praxis gives this aptitude because as first object it includes principles and through them conclusions, not as end. As end it gives nothing except as loved and desired and moving the agent; but it includes such principles before being loved, since the truth of necessary practical principles depends no more on the will than speculative ones. Also, anything else that virtually contained such knowledge would give the same conformity, e.g. the praxis itself or what it concerns; thus man, not happiness or health, may be the subject of moral science and medicine, since the ratio of each end is included in man.
claims: The end grounds practical knowledge as object, not as end.
The truth of necessary practical principles does not depend on the will.
Whatever virtually contains practical knowledge grounds its conformity.
concepts: man as subject of ethics and medicine

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2192.summary: Objection: practical first principles are always taken from the end, so the end always first virtually contains their knowledge. Even if granted, it would hold as object, not as end; man would then be end of health and natural happiness, though not the proximate end of praxis. Or the antecedent, true particularly, should be denied universally: it holds where the ratio of end is not concluded from something belonging to practical knowledge.
claims: Even if practical principles are always taken from the end, the end grounds them as object.
Practical principles are not universally taken from the end.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2240.summary: Alternatively, the claim that first practical principles come from the end holds among principles taken from moral circumstances once an act good in kind is presupposed, since then the object is not a circumstance. Taking the act bare, the object too is a circumstance, and since the first circumstance of an act seems prior to all others, the object that first specifies the act as good in kind, to be further qualified by other circumstances, seems first in practical knowledge. Whether this succeeds is left to book III.
claims: Taken barely, the object is the first circumstance specifying an act as good in kind.
The object seems prior to the end in practical knowledge.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2292.summary: Summary of the third article: practical science does not have its first extension from the end as end, for the reasons given.
claims: Practical science's extension does not come from the end as end.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2311.summary: Solution of the second question: Scotus holds the negative, that a science is not practical per se from ordering to praxis as end. The first relation, conformity, comes per se from the object, which is the rectitude of the praxis or something virtually including it; so praxis can be conformed to that knowledge to be right, as knowledge is of its object.
claims: A science is not practical per se from its ordering to praxis as end.
Conformity comes from the object, which is or virtually includes the rectitude of praxis.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2341.summary: On the other relation, priority: some cognition necessarily naturally precedes praxis, from the natural order of intellect and will. But the prior intellection is practical only when it determines the rectitude of the praxis, formally or virtually. If the prior apprehension determines nothing about rectitude, there is priority without conformity. If it determines rectitude but the power whose praxis it is cannot be determined by anything else, the knowledge is determinative but not conformative, lacking prior conformity as a directing rule, and so not fully practical.
claims: Intellection naturally precedes praxis.
Prior intellection is practical only if it determines the rectitude of praxis.
If the practicing power cannot be regulated from outside, the knowledge is not fully practical.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2424.summary: So, although cognition is absolutely prior by the nature of intellect and will, prior conforming cognition depends jointly on the object, the order of powers, and the practicing power, the will, being in some way regulable from outside. If the object determines the intellect to know rectitude before the will wills, and the will is regulable, there is prior conforming apprehension. This happens whenever the rectitude of praxis is a necessary knowable, as principle by understanding or as conclusion by science.
claims: Prior conforming cognition requires object, order of powers, and a regulable will.
It occurs whenever the rectitude of praxis is necessarily knowable.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2472.summary: These points about the two relations should be understood generally, unless for the divine intellect something must be added, namely whether the practicing power must be determinable by something prior or conformable to it as rule. Whether this is required is addressed in the reply to the fourth objection against the solution of the main question.
claims: Whether practical knowledge requires a regulable will is reserved for the divine case.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2512.summary: When determinate rectitude belongs to a praxis contingently, no object determines the intellect to know it before the will wills, speaking of intellect and will in general, since the contingent is not determined to either side before every act of will. For a particular intellect and will, conforming cognition can precede the praxis in one whose will does not first determine its rectitude, but not in every intelligent being.
claims: Contingent rectitude is not determined before any act of will.
Conforming knowledge of contingent rectitude can precede only in an agent whose will does not first determine it.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2562.summary: Example: the rectitude of loving God is right and necessary and virtually included in the ratio of God. In anyone, this praxis is preceded not only by apprehension but by conforming apprehension to which it must conform to be right.
claims: The rectitude of loving God is necessary and contained in the concept of God.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2587.summary: So from an object that of itself determines the intellect to know determinate rectitude, and from the order of intellect and will, prior conforming knowledge arises, wherever rectitude necessarily belongs. But the rectitude of worshipping God by the sacrifice of the altar is contingent: right now, not in the Old Testament. No object determines knowledge of it before every act of will, so such knowledge precedes not every will but only one that does not first determine it, like the human will; its rectitude is determined by the divine will accepting this worship now and not at other times.
claims: Necessary rectitude grounds conforming knowledge prior to any will.
Contingent rectitude, such as eucharistic worship, is determined by the divine will.
Such knowledge precedes the human will but not the divine.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2654.summary: Turning to the first question, Scotus reports five ways holding the negative. The first (Henry of Ghent's) distinguishes the will's act that perfects it (concerning the end, by which it unites itself to the ultimate end) from the act perfected by it (concerning means, tending outward). The first needs no directive, only display of the object, and belongs to speculative science; the second needs direction and belongs to practical science. Since theology principally intends the act concerning the end, it is most perfectly speculative.
claims: On this view, the will's act regarding the end needs only display of the object, not direction.
Theology principally intends that act, so it is speculative.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2759.summary: Supporting authority for the first way: Augustine says all our works are so that the eye by which God is seen may be cleansed.
claims: Our works are ordered to the vision of God (Augustine).

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2777.summary: Further argument: no directive is needed where there can be no error; practical science is directive; the blessed cannot err, so their science is not practical, nor is ours, being the same.
claims: Direction is needed only where error is possible.
The blessed cannot err, so their theology is not practical.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2799.summary: Further argument from this author's view elsewhere: God has no practical science, yet he has this science most of all, or alone; so it is not practical.
claims: God has no practical science, but has theology most of all.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2813.summary: Scotus turns the first way's reasoning against it, in four ways. First: even if the will cannot err about the end shown universally, it can, by their own account, err about the end shown particularly, so right action about it requires directive display. Theology shows the end in particular, the universal display belonging to metaphysics. So even if the blessed cannot err about the theological object absolutely, they can in some act, and need directive knowledge.
claims: The will can err about the end shown in particular.
Theology shows the end in particular, so requires directive knowledge.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2870.summary: Second: a directive habit is posited not for the substance of an act but for its circumstances, as temperance for eating. So even if the will were determined as to the substance of its act toward the end, direction would be needed for the circumstances. Wherever one can err or act rightly in praxis, practical knowledge is needed; in love of the end as theological, error is possible both regarding the object shown in particular and the act's circumstances.
claims: Directive habits concern circumstances, not the substance of acts.
Love of the end can err in object and circumstances, so needs practical knowledge.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2929.summary: Third: what is principally intended to be loved outside the genus of cognition is principally intended to be known within it. On their view love of the end is principally intended, so knowledge of the end is principally intended; but every science principally intends knowledge of its first subject, so the end is this science's principal subject. Practical principles are taken from the end and conclude practical conclusions, so this science, which first intends love of the end, is practical.
claims: What is principally loved is principally known.
The end is theology's principal subject; practical principles derive from it, so theology is practical.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e2979.summary: Fourth: principles and conclusions belong to the same genus, practical or speculative; practical conclusions resolve to practical principles. Knowledge of the end directs acts concerning means, and knowledge of means is included in knowledge of the end as principle; so if knowledge of means is practical, knowledge of the end is practical. This answers their first reason: the will is not determined of itself (first two arguments), and even if it were, the knowledge would still be practical (last two).
claims: Practical conclusions resolve to practical principles.
Knowledge of the end, as principle of knowledge of means, is practical.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3034.summary: On Augustine's authority: it seems to conclude that vision of God is this science's end, which they do not grant. Rather, Augustine speaks of exterior works (fasting, vigils, prayers), since any exterior act is apt to conform to an interior act from which it has its goodness and is ultimately ordered to willing.
claims: Augustine's text concerns exterior works, which are ordered to interior acts and ultimately to willing.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3073.summary: Reply to the argument from error: as an agent per se intends to induce a form and only per accidens removes the contrary, so a habit per se directs and per accidens excludes error. A perfect habit admits no error. The blessed cannot err, but they still have a directive habit; without it, per impossibile, they could err, and with it, by its perfection, all error is excluded.
claims: A habit directs per se and excludes error only per accidens.
The blessed's inerrancy is due to their perfect directive habit.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3113.summary: The reply to the fourth argument (God has no practical science) is deferred to the reply to the fourth objection after the solution of the first question.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3128.summary: Second way: although love of the end can be elicited rightly or not, it is not praxis, since it does not concern a contingent object. Averroes (Ethics I) defines praxis as operation according to choice, and choice concerns only contingents (Ethics III), being deliberative appetite. Hence Scotus's description of praxis is insufficient for omitting the object, and no knowledge extending only to volition of the ultimate end is practical.
claims: On this view, praxis is operation according to choice, which concerns only contingents.
Love of the ultimate end is not praxis.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3176.summary: Against the second way: the fourth argument against the first way applies. Also, praxis is the operation to which an appetitive virtue inclines, since every virtue is an elective habit (Ethics II), and choice is praxis. Not only charity but acquired habitual love, an appetitive habit consonant with right reason, inclines to love of the end. The way's motive will be answered in reply to the second principal argument.
claims: Virtue inclines to praxis; acquired love and charity incline to love of the end, so it is praxis.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3222.summary: Third way: either volition is not properly praxis, only acts posterior to it, or it is praxis only in relation to some act commanded in a lower power (sensory appetite, motive power).
claims: On this view, volition is praxis only derivatively or through commanded acts.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3246.summary: Argument for the third way: all praxis follows choice. Ethics VI: choice is the principle of action as effective, not final; an effective principle naturally precedes its effect.
claims: Choice is the efficient principle of action and precedes it.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3273.summary: Further: practical habits are generated from praxes, and practical habits are generated from acts following choice, so those are praxes.
claims: Practical habits are generated from acts following choice.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3286.summary: Further: Averroes on Ethics I says praxis is operation according to choice, so praxis follows choice.
claims: Praxis is operation according to choice (Averroes).

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3302.summary: Against the third way's claim that only acts following choice are praxis: Ethics VI says there is no right choice without right reason and a virtuous habit, so virtue is required per se for right choice. It would not be if virtue were generated from acts posterior to choice, since then it would incline per se only to those acts.
claims: Virtue is required per se for right choice.
So virtue is not generated only from acts posterior to choice.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3336.summary: Same point in another form: a habit is generated from the acts it inclines to (Ethics II); moral virtue inclines per se to right choice, being an elective habit; so moral virtue is generated per se from choices, and not only acts following choice are praxis.
claims: Moral virtue, an elective habit, is generated from choices.
Choices themselves are praxis.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3375.summary: Moreover, as the first article proved, the elicited act of will is primarily praxis, and the commanded act only because of it. So a choice alone, without ordering to a commanded act (e.g. lacking matter for outward action), is truly praxis. Example: someone without money who imagines money and chooses to distribute it liberally if he had it completes the choice from which liberality is generated or which liberality elicits; no further outward pursuit is required when the matter of the outward act is lacking.
claims: A choice is praxis even without a following commanded act.
A virtuous choice about an imagined object can generate or express virtue.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3441.summary: Further: the ordering of choice to the commanded act can only be that of cause to effect; it is unfitting that a cause be such not of itself, as prior to the effect, but only because it is actually ordered to producing it, since a cause has nothing from its effect or from its ordering to it.
claims: A cause does not derive its character from its effect.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3472.summary: Reply to the authority from Ethics VI: Aristotle adds that the principle of choice is appetite and practical reason, so right choice requires virtue in appetite, and that there is no right choice without moral habit; so virtue has an elicited act more immediate to it than the act of which choice is the commanding principle. The elicited act of will, choice, is a good action before the commanded outward act is good, as Aristotle's next words show (good action is not without character). Scotus grants that choice is the effective principle of action, since the commanded act is moral, but not that only that act is praxis; choice is prior praxis, by which the other is good praxis.
claims: Choice is a good action before the commanded act is good.
Choice is the effective principle of the commanded act, and itself prior praxis.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3564.summary: Reply to the second argument: practical habit is generated from choices, as with one who often chooses to give liberally, which could generate liberality even without commanded acts when means are lacking. Yet when commanded acts are impossible, the will does not commonly choose rightly and often about their matter (one does not will, or wills weakly, what one thinks impossible, per Augustine); so virtue is commonly not generated without commanded acts following choice, though it is generated not from those but from the choices, in which moral goodness is formally, whereas in commanded acts it is only materially.
claims: Practical habits are generated from choices.
Moral goodness is formally in choices and only materially in commanded acts.
In practice, virtue usually develops alongside commanded acts because one does not strongly will the impossible.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3623.summary: Reply to Averroes' definition: 'according to choice' cannot mark efficient causality if the definition is to be convertible with the defined, as Ethics VI shows; it means effectively or formally. Or 'choice' means freedom or denominative power, or the eliciting of the act of willing, which is not a choice or volition but an action in the category of Action. According to such 'choice', as active principle, every praxis exists, whether a choice or following one, since action in the category of Action reduces to an effective principle.
claims: 'According to choice' must be read as formal or as referring to freedom or to the eliciting action, not narrowly as efficient cause.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3671.summary: Summary: these three ways hold theology purely speculative despite its extension to love of the end, whether because the will is naturally determined to it once the object is shown, or because, though free, it does not concern a contingent doable object, or because, whatever the object, it rests in its own elicited act without ordering to a commanded act.
claims: The first three ways all hold theology purely speculative for different reasons.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3708.summary: Persuasion for these ways: extension to love cannot make knowledge practical, or all knowledge would be practical, since every knowledge is followed by some love or delight.
claims: All knowledge is followed by some love or delight.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3724.summary: Also: Ethics X says the happy person is most loved by God (or most loving of God), yet Aristotle holds that happiness speculative, not practical.
claims: Aristotle places happiness, which involves love of God, in speculation.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3741.summary: Against the common conclusion of the three ways: it would follow that some operation is in man's power, a genuinely human act, yet neither speculation nor praxis, namely love of the end, which seems absurd.
claims: Love of the end is a human act that must be either speculation or praxis.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3763.summary: Further: it is unfitting that knowledge directive of any volition not be practical, since truth in agreement with right appetite is the proper work of the practical mind (Ethics VI).
claims: Knowledge directive of volition is practical, as truth agreeing with right appetite.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3789.summary: Reply to the argument from delight: delight is a passion naturally following perfect operation; no knowledge is practical through extension to it, since it is not properly praxis (see III d.15). But loving or desiring the known object, with this or that circumstance, is truly praxis, not naturally consequent on apprehension but freely elicitable, rightly or not.
claims: Delight is a natural passion following operation, not praxis.
Loving the known object is free, can be right or wrong, and so is praxis.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3828.summary: Reply to Ethics X: the text does not compel, since 'Dei amantissimus' is passive (most loved by God), not active, as the continuation shows: if the gods care for humans and rejoice in what is best and most akin to them, the intellect, they will reward those who love it as friends.
claims: Aristotle's phrase means most loved by God, not most loving God.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3862.summary: Setting the text aside, does Aristotle's speculatively happy person love the end, as distinct from delighting? Metaphysics XII: the first mover moves as loved, so the lower intelligence loves the first; yet he places its happiness in speculation. So he includes love, not just delight, under speculation, and extension to love would not make knowledge practical for him.
claims: For Aristotle, the intelligences love the first mover yet their happiness is speculative.
Aristotle includes love under speculation.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3916.summary: Why not follow Aristotle then, since the ratio of practical and speculative comes from him, and the first two ways seem to follow him well? Because the love he posits in the intelligence is by natural necessity of the will, with no possibility of erring or acting rightly, so knowledge of it would be only ostensive, not directive as to the object in particular, its conditions, or the circumstances of willing.
claims: For Aristotle the intelligence's love is naturally necessary, so the relevant knowledge is merely ostensive.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e3960.summary: Theologians do not say this of intellectual creatures' love of God in particular and as to circumstances. Had Aristotle agreed that love of the end can be elicited freely, rightly or not, and is right only if it conforms to right reason both showing the object and dictating how to elicit it, he would perhaps have held such knowledge practical. So the theologian, who disagrees with him in the minor premiss, should consistently disagree in the conclusion rather than agree in a conclusion he would not have drawn had he held the theologian's minor.
claims: Creaturely love of God is free and can be right or wrong.
Given that premiss, Aristotle's own criteria make theology practical.
Theologians should not adopt Aristotle's conclusion while rejecting his premiss.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4017.summary: So we agree with Aristotle on the major: knowledge is speculative if, though it extends to love by showing the object, it is in no way directive of the act as circumstantiable and as concerning this object in particular. We deny the minor in this case. Even if he posited such necessity in the intelligence's love, would he posit it in the human sage's will, whom he does not hold naturally happy? If not, that will can be directed, and he denies practical knowledge only because he held happiness speculative.
claims: Knowledge that only shows an object and in no way directs the act is speculative.
For theology this condition fails, since the act needs direction.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4069.summary: Fourth way: theology is affective. Acceptable if affective is a kind of practical; but if affective is a third member besides practical and speculative, it contradicts the first article, where love was shown to be true praxis, and many authorities that divide sciences only into speculative and practical.
claims: 'Affective' is acceptable only as a kind of practical.
There is no third member besides speculative and practical.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4106.summary: Fifth way: theology is contemplative, citing Augustine (De Trinitate XII) that wisdom relates to contemplation and science to action; theology is wisdom, so contemplative, not practical. Reply: Augustine says the higher and lower portions of the soul differ only by function, and each contains a trinity (memory, understanding, will), the higher bearing the image of the uncreated Trinity. Only the higher is contemplative, since it regards eternal things; so this contemplation is not limited to speculation within the genus of knowledge but includes will, and can extend beyond knowledge just as the active portion can. Theology can be contemplative in Augustine's sense and still practical, if it extends to praxis in the higher portion.
claims: Augustine's contemplation includes will as well as intellect.
Being contemplative in Augustine's sense does not exclude being practical.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4197.summary: Another opinion concludes differently: theology is both speculative and practical. First argument: as a book containing some law and some philosophy, whether separately or mixed, would be both, so this teaching treats speculative and practical matters mixed together.
claims: A doctrine mixing speculative and practical matters is both.
concepts: theology as both speculative and practical

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4244.summary: Second argument: no speculative science treats operables more distinctly than speculation requires, nor practical science speculables more than praxis requires; this science treats both more distinctly than the other would require, as distinctly as if about each alone; so it is both.
claims: Theology treats operables and speculables each in their own right, so is both speculative and practical.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4303.summary: Against it: a habit without evidence from its object is not distinguished by distinction of objects (else there would be two infused faiths); this habit lacks such evidence, so it is not two habits on account of operables and speculables.
claims: A habit lacking evidence from its object is not divided by objects.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4334.summary: Further: the two-habit view may have some plausibility for theology as given in Scripture, but not for theology in itself, whose first subject is the divine essence as this. Of this subject, being most truly one knowable, there is apt to be first one truly unified knowledge; knowledge first of something else would not be theology in itself. So theology is simply one habit, though Scripture may contain other knowledge about other subjects.
claims: Theology in itself, having a single subject, is one habit.
Scripture may contain other knowledge besides theology.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4385.summary: Also, the order of sciences by eminence ends in one alone, since there cannot be two simply first sciences. This single most eminent science is theology, which alone is first about the first subject.
claims: There is only one simply first science, theology.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4407.summary: Scotus turns the second argument: knowledge is practical if it treats speculables no more than practical knowledge or praxis requires; theology does just that. Any knowledge of the conditions of the end's desirability, of the means as means, and of anything about which the operative power can err unless directed is necessary for practical knowledge, and all knowledge given here of the end and the means is such, or at least the will can err about it in ignorance.
claims: Knowledge of the end's desirability and of means is necessary for practical knowledge.
All theological knowledge is of this kind.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4479.summary: Illustrations: although the Trinity does not make the end more desirable (God is end as one God, not as triune), a will ignorant of the Trinity may err in loving or desiring, e.g. desiring to enjoy one person alone. Ignorance that God made the world may lead to failing to return the gratitude due for so great a sharing of goodness; ignorance of the articles of redemption may lead to failing to return due love for so great a benefit; and so with other theological truths.
claims: Ignorance of the Trinity can lead to disordered love of God.
Knowledge of creation and redemption grounds due gratitude and love.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4527.summary: The assumption is evident: whatever conditions are taught about the end are apt rather to show its desirability, and conditions of means to show their ordering to the end.
claims: Theological teaching about the end shows its desirability; about means, their ordering.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4547.summary: Reply to their argument: the minor is false. The end and means cannot be treated so distinctly that the whole knowledge is not practical for a created intellect, since all of it shows the end as desirable, the means as ordered, or anything about which an undirected will could err.
claims: All theological knowledge is practical for a created intellect.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4587.summary: Another opinion reaches the same conclusion (theology both speculative and practical) while holding theology to be simply one habit.
claims: On this view, theology is one habit, both speculative and practical.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4603.summary: Against it: when something common is first divided by opposed differences, both cannot be found in one thing under it, or the same body could be corporeal and incorporeal or the same man rational and irrational. Science in general is first divided into practical and speculative (Avicenna, Averroes, Gundissalinus), so both cannot be in one science. Also contradictories would follow, extending and not extending.
claims: Opposed differences dividing a genus cannot coexist in one species.
Practical and speculative are such differences, so no single science is both.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4668.summary: Scotus's answer to the first question: since the elicited act of will is truly praxis even without a commanded act, and practical extension consists in aptitudinal conformity and priority, knowledge is practical if aptitudinally conformable to right volition and naturally prior to it. All necessary theology in a created intellect is such. Its first subject is virtually conformable to right volition, since the first principles of rectitude in willing are taken from its ratio, and it determines the created intellect to know the rectitude of praxis for all necessary theological truths naturally before any created will wills. So theology is practical. Confirmation: its first object is the ultimate end, and principles taken from the ultimate end are practical, so its conclusions are too.
claims: Knowledge is practical if aptitudinally conformable and naturally prior to right volition.
Theology's first subject virtually contains the principles of right willing.
All necessary theology in a created intellect is practical.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4768.summary: Objection: as the previous question showed, God is first subject here not as end but as this essence, while practical principles are those taken from the end as end.
claims: Theology's subject is God as this essence, not as end.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4786.summary: Objection: knowledge of the ultimate end is not, and is not apt to be, immediately conformable to praxis to be elicited, so it is not proximately practical.
claims: Knowledge of the ultimate end is not immediately conformable to praxis.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4799.summary: Objection: the first object virtually includes conformity to right praxis but not only such knowledge, else there could be no speculative knowledge of it. How is 'God is triune' or 'the Father generates the Son' practical? So the first object includes speculative knowledge, and many of the most properly theological truths (as distinct from metaphysics) are speculative.
claims: Truths like 'God is triune' seem speculative.
The first object includes speculative knowledge.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4849.summary: Objection: then God's science, about the same first subject, would be practical, as the reasoning seems to apply to the divine intellect as to the created.
claims: The argument would make God's theology practical.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4867.summary: Reply to the first objection: principles in a science are taken not from the relation of end but from the absolute in which that relation is founded, which is this essence.
claims: Practical principles are taken from the absolute foundation of the end-relation, the divine essence.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4885.summary: Reply to the second: what virtually contains conforming knowledge is virtually conformable, so its knowledge is practical, since practical conclusions have practical principles. The knowledge proximate to it, concerning the end, is knowledge of enjoyment of the end, which is apt to be formally conformable to the praxis of enjoyment.
claims: What virtually contains conforming knowledge is itself practical.
Knowledge of enjoyment of the end is formally conformable to the act of enjoyment.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4915.summary: Reply to the third: the first object includes only knowledge conformable to right volition, since by its virtue nothing is known of it that is not either the rectitude of some volition or virtually including knowledge of it. Scotus grants the consequence that there can be no speculative science of it: knowledge of it and of anything intrinsic known through it is necessarily aptitudinally conformable to praxis, and prior if what is known is necessary.
claims: Everything known by virtue of theology's first object bears on the rectitude of volition.
There can be no speculative science of God as this essence.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4956.summary: On 'God is triune' and 'the Father generates the Son': these are practical. The first virtually includes knowledge of the rectitude of love directed to three persons, so that an act directed to one alone excluding the others (as an unbeliever might elicit) would not be right. The second includes knowledge of rectitude as the act concerns two persons, one from the other.
claims: Trinitarian truths are practical because they govern the rectitude of love of God.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e4993.summary: Objection: only the essential is the ratio terminating the act of love, else there would be lovability in one person not in another, and none would be blessed in itself. Theology is more properly about personal than essential features, since many essentials are known in metaphysics; so as distinct from metaphysics it is not practical.
claims: Only the divine essence is the formal ratio of lovability.
Theology's proper content is personal, so would not be practical.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5032.summary: Reply: the essential is the formal ratio terminating love as that on account of which; the persons terminate it as those who are loved. Rectitude requires not only a fitting formal ratio in the object but also a fitting object in which it is; so beyond what the essential includes, the personal includes further proper knowledge of the rectitude required.
claims: The essence is loved as the ratio, the persons as the objects loved.
Right love requires both a fitting ratio and a fitting object.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5076.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: it could probably be granted that God's theology of necessary truths is practical, since in his intellect the first theological object generates knowledge conformable to right volition and naturally prior to it. Prior because the intellect naturally understands the first object before the will wills it, and so can have all knowledge virtually included in that intellection before willing, even, per impossibile, with all volition excluded. A second proof, that the divine intellect does not reason discursively and so knows all included truths together with the first object, is weaker.
claims: God's theology of necessary truths can be granted to be practical.
The divine intellect understands its first object naturally before the will wills it.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5163.summary: Objection: then the divine will would not be the first rule of its own acts, if knowledge to which it must conform to act rightly precedes its act. This removes the will's supreme freedom, since it would be determined by another and not first by itself in its first act; and if practical knowledge precedes all its acts, the will is determined by the intellect to its first act, since it cannot dissent, or it could sin.
claims: Prior practical knowledge would undermine the divine will's being its own first rule and its freedom.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5200.summary: Further objection: it was said that Aristotle rightly concludes that if an intelligence naturally loves God seen, knowledge showing God is not practical. The same inference holds of God, who naturally loves himself.
claims: God loves himself naturally, so knowledge of himself is not practical by the same reasoning.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5220.summary: Further objection: a director is in some way a cause of what it directs, so they are really distinct; but God's understanding is not really distinct from his willing. Also, the intellect directs only an act yet to be elicited, as prior to it; but in God willing himself does not follow the will in being, so it is never as if to be elicited, always as if elicited; so there is no direction.
claims: Direction requires real distinction between director and directed.
God's self-willing is never 'to be elicited', so cannot be directed.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5253.summary: First line of reply: taking 'rule' as what makes praxis right, the first rule is the ultimate end, which first virtually contains knowledge of all necessary rectitude of any praxis, as the first subject of a speculative science contains all speculative truths. This rule rectifies intellect and will in their natural order, generating conforming knowledge before rectifying the praxis; so there is a prior power rightly ordered before the practicing power, and the first consequence (that the divine will is not the first rule) seems to be granted.
claims: The first rule of right praxis is the ultimate end, which virtually contains all necessary rectitude.
It rectifies intellect before will, following their natural order.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5312.summary: To the claim that this removes supreme freedom: as freedom in general is compatible with prior apprehension, so supreme freedom is compatible with supreme prior apprehension; and the most perfect apprehension of a praxis includes knowledge of its conformity when that belongs to it necessarily.
claims: Supreme freedom is compatible with supreme prior apprehension.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5334.summary: To the claim that the will is determined from outside: deny it, of determination by a sufficient agent. Though the divine will cannot dissent from prior rectifying knowledge, this is not because the intellect is a sufficient active cause determining it, but from the will's perfection, by which it acts in conformity with the prior power when that power has first acted perfectly on the object, knowing as much as it can. This does not hold for contingents, of which the divine intellect lacks full knowledge before every act of will; with necessary knowables it always holds, since they are perfectly known without any act of will.
claims: The divine will's conformity to prior knowledge comes from its own perfection, not determination by the intellect.
For contingents the divine intellect has no complete knowledge prior to the will.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5413.summary: Alternative answer, which Scotus seems to favour: necessary theology in the divine intellect is not practical, since intellection is not naturally prior to volition as conforming or directing. Even if knowledge of rectitude could of itself conform a power rectifiable from outside, the divine will is rectified with respect to its first object by itself alone, whether it tends naturally or freely, never indifferent to rectitude or receiving it from elsewhere. So it requires only display of the object, not directive knowledge; if display alone preceded and knowledge of rectitude followed, the volition would be as right as now.
claims: God's necessary theology is not practical, because the divine will is rectified by itself alone.
The divine will requires only display of its object, not direction.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5510.summary: So to the argument for the priority of rectitude: though intellection is somehow prior to volition, it is not prior as right reason prior to praxis, which would be the priority of rule to ruled, impossible where the will is wholly its own rule. The whole controversy about whether God's self-knowledge is practical comes down to this: whether knowledge directive of itself is practical even when the knower's practicing power is not directable, or not practical because it is not directable. Whichever side one takes, one should argue consistently.
claims: Where the will is wholly its own rule, intellection is not prior as rule to ruled.
The dispute turns on whether directive knowledge is practical when the will cannot be directed.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5567.summary: Second article of the main question: whether theology of contingents is practical. It can be practical only in an intellect able to have determinative knowledge of the rectitude of praxis before the praxis is elicited, since only there can it be conformable and prior. Only created intellects are such, since no created will first determines the contingent rectitude of a praxis.
claims: Theology of contingents is practical only in an intellect that knows the rectitude before the praxis.
Only created intellects meet this condition, since no created will first determines contingent rectitude.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5605.summary: So in the divine intellect theology of contingents cannot be practical, given two assumptions: that practical knowledge and its praxis must belong to the same supposit, and that God's only praxis is volition (no third power besides intellect and will). For no knowledge conformable to a right contingent volition precedes God's volition, since that volition first determines the rectitude.
claims: Practical knowledge and its praxis belong to the same supposit.
God's only praxis is volition.
God's will first determines contingent rectitude, so no prior conforming knowledge exists in God.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5642.summary: The first assumption is doubtful but can be defended. If any knowledge of another's praxis were practical, my knowledge that God creates the world or that an intelligence moves a heaven would be practical, which seems false. At least, an inferior intellect could not have practical knowledge of a praxis that a superior performs with no contribution from the inferior; likewise for superior or equal, unless they contribute, in which case they have a praxis of their own.
claims: Knowledge of another's praxis is not practical for the knower.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5693.summary: Further support: if practical knowledge has some causality on the praxis it extends to, and is apt to have it primarily only on praxis in the knower, the point follows.
claims: Practical knowledge's causality reaches primarily the knower's own praxis.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5713.summary: Objection: then about the same thing one intellect would have practical knowledge and another speculative, if the praxis were possible to one and not the other.
claims: The same knowledge would be practical for one and speculative for another.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5726.summary: Reply (rejecting the first assumption): perfect rectitude of praxis includes the circumstance of the agent. 'God is to be loved' is not completely practical unless 'by a will' is added, since God is not to be loved by a brute. 'God is to be loved by a will' is practical in any intellect; 'man must sometimes fast' is practical for angels and God too, and 'the heaven is to be moved by an angel' for man and God. Scotus accepts the consequence the first proof treated as absurd.
claims: Perfect rectitude of praxis includes the agent as a circumstance.
Fully specified practical truths are practical in any intellect.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5772.summary: Objection: then priority of practical knowledge to praxis fails, since God's love of himself is right before man or angel can understand that God is to be loved by a will. Reply: the priority must come from object and intellect: the object is apt of itself to determine any intellect to know the praxis's determinate rectitude before the praxis, even if some intellect, through imperfection, is not determined before the operating power acts through its perfection.
claims: Priority of practical knowledge is a priority from the object, not of actual time in every intellect.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5829.summary: Reply to the other objection: as the will can be a superior cause of a motive power's praxis only within the same agent (mine not of an angel's motive power), so if practical knowledge causes praxis, it is within the same knower and agent. But knowledge need not be non-practical in another, unless 'practical' is taken strictly as immediately applicable to work through identity of knower and agent, as when 'to know' is construed with an infinitive of praxis: only God knows how to love himself infinitely, though an angel knows he is to be infinitely loved by himself.
claims: Causal practicality operates within one agent, but practical knowledge can exist in another intellect.
Strictly practical knowledge is immediately applicable through identity of knower and agent.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5879.summary: Whoever answers this way must grant that all truths about the praxis of created agents are known practically by any intellect, since, necessary from the object or contingent from elsewhere, they are apt to conform to and determine the rectitude of those praxes before they are elicited. Necessary truths about the divine will are practical, but contingent ones not, since they have no conformity before the praxis: God knows practically that man should repent or that an angel should move the heaven, but not that God should will a holy man to repent or an angel to move the heaven.
claims: Truths about creatures' praxis are practical in any intellect.
Necessary truths about the divine will are practical; contingent ones are not.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5943.summary: What is theology of contingents in itself, not relative to an intellect? It is as it is from its object, and from its object it is not conformable to praxis before any praxis, since the object yields no knowledge of determinate contingent rectitude. So it is not practical from its object, hence speculative if the division is exhaustive. This fits denying it is practical in God, since it is in itself as it is in the perfect instance of the genus.
claims: Theology of contingents in itself, from its object, is speculative.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e5983.summary: Objection: then knowledge speculative in itself is practical for some, e.g. the created intellect, so practical does not exclude speculative. Reply: being speculative from the object is being per se speculative; being practical from an object that sufficiently determines the intellect to know rectitude is being per se practical, before any volition; these are opposed as extensible and non-extensible to praxis. Being practical from elsewhere, from an extrinsic cause like a will determining the intellect, is being accidentally practical. So theology of contingents is practical for us, though speculative in itself.
claims: Per se practicality comes from the object; accidental practicality from an extrinsic cause like the divine will.
Theology of contingents is per se speculative but accidentally practical for us.
concepts: per se and per accidens practical

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6044.summary: Objection: what has one opposite per se cannot have the other per se or per accidens. Reply: granting this in the first or second mode of per se (not the third, meaning 'solitarily'), the opposite of 'per se speculative' does not inhere in any way, for theology of contingents is per se speculative in the second mode. But 'per accidens practical' is not opposed to it, as being black simply and white in a respect are not opposed. 'It is per se per se speculative' is granted, and 'per accidens practical' does not conflict with that predicate.
claims: 'Per se speculative' and 'per accidens practical' are not opposed, like 'black simply' and 'white in a respect'.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6118.summary: If either of the two assumptions is rejected: theology of contingents, though not practical in itself, would be accidentally practical in every created and uncreated intellect, since in the divine intellect it can conform to praxis before the creature's will elicits it; God knows the adult sinner under the new law ought to be contrite before the sinner is. Rejecting the first assumption, God's knowledge of another's praxis is practical. Rejecting the second, if God's action ad extra is a praxis formally other than volition, though God's intellect does not know A is to be created before his will wills it, it knows A before creating it; so conforming knowledge precedes outward praxis, conformable not from the object but from elsewhere.
claims: Rejecting either assumption makes contingent theology accidentally practical in God too.
God knows what the sinner ought to do before the sinner acts.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6187.summary: Scotus's firm position: theology of contingents is not per se, i.e. from its object, practical, but can be accidentally practical in a created intellect whose operation follows a praxis whose rectitude is determined by the divine will. Whether it is practical for the divine intellect follows from holding the two assumptions or their opposites.
claims: Theology of contingents is not per se practical.
It can be accidentally practical in a created intellect whose praxis has rectitude determined by the divine will.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6219.summary: Three probable theses: practical knowledge rectifies praxis about contingents; it rectifies a practicing power rectifiable from outside itself; and in God the only practicing power is the will. From the first and third, divine practical knowledge would rectify the divine will, which the second excludes, since the divine will first wills rightly regarding its first object of itself, and about contingents is determined by itself alone, not by prior knowledge of rectitude.
claims: Practical knowledge rectifies a power that is rectifiable from outside.
God's will is self-rectifying, so God has no practical knowledge in this sense.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6269.summary: Reply to the first principal argument: faith is not a speculative habit, nor belief a speculative act, nor the vision following belief speculative; it is practical, being apt to conform to enjoyment (fruitio) and to be had naturally first in the created intellect, so that right enjoyment may be elicited in conformity with it.
claims: Faith, belief and the beatific vision are practical, not speculative.
The vision is ordered to right enjoyment of God.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6305.summary: Reply to the second: the contingent that practical science concerns is the end or what is for the end. In doable matters action is the ultimate end (Ethics VI), so the contingency of the action suffices for practical science or its object.
claims: The contingency of the action suffices for practical science.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6330.summary: Objection: science is of necessary things (Posterior Analytics I), so there is no science of contingents.
claims: Science is only of the necessary.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6346.summary: Objection: Ethics distinguishes the scientific from the calculative part by necessary and contingent; science belongs to the scientific part, so it is about the necessary.
claims: Habits of the scientific part concern the necessary.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6365.summary: Objection: if theology concerns contingent doables, it is an active habit with true reason, which is the definition of prudence (Ethics VI); so theology is prudence, not science.
claims: A habit about contingent doables with true reason is prudence.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6383.summary: Reply to the first two: there are many necessary truths about contingents, since of an act contingently elicited it is necessarily concluded what it must be to be right. There is science of it as to the necessarily demonstrated conclusion, though the act is contingent as elicited by its power. So 'science is of the necessary' means of a necessary predicate said of a contingent. Similarly the calculative habit concerns the act as contingently elicited, science the same act as something is necessarily concluded about it; how one object can belong to several habits is treated later.
claims: There are necessary truths about contingent acts, namely what they must be to be right.
Science of contingents concerns necessary conclusions about them.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6473.summary: Reply to the third: the same argument would make moral science prudence, since it is an active habit with true reason. The definition of prudence must be understood of the proximate active habit acquired from acts. As art relates to the expert's habit in making, so moral science relates to prudence in doing: art and moral science are remote and universal, prudence and expertise particular and proximate. Otherwise no science would be practical, contrary to Aristotle and Avicenna.
claims: Prudence is the proximate, particular active habit acquired from acts.
Moral science and art are universal, remote directive habits.
