jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6545.summary: Reply to the Boethius argument: by 'theology' Boethius means metaphysics, and what he says of God's substance means God is considered there as far as possible in acquired sciences.
claims: Boethius's speculative 'theology' is metaphysics.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6569.summary: Reply to the nobility argument: it belongs to nobility for the lower to reach its superior (Politics VII), as human sense is nobler than animal sense for being ordered to intellect; so it is noble for a science to be ordered to the act of a nobler power. Aristotle posits no science conformable to a will's praxis about the end, since he takes the will's relation to the end as a simple natural motion, not praxis. Had he posited praxis about the end, he would not have denied that practical science about it is nobler than speculative. We hold there is true praxis about the end, so practical knowledge about the end is nobler than any speculative; the premiss drawn from Metaphysics I must be denied.
claims: Being ordered to a nobler power's act ennobles a science.
There is true praxis about the end, and practical knowledge of it is nobler than any speculative knowledge.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6659.summary: On the first proof (speculative science is for its own sake): a science for its own sake is nobler than one for the sake of a lower act. Every science Aristotle called practical is for something lower than speculation, at least about a lower object, so some speculative science is nobler than each. But a science for the sake of an act nobler than its own act is not less noble for that ordering, otherwise our senses would be less noble than animals'.
claims: A science ordered to a nobler act is not ennobled less for that ordering.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6703.summary: On certainty: every scientific cognition is equally certain proportionally, since each resolves to its immediate principles, but not in quantity. Since the objects of Aristotle's practical sciences are less knowable in themselves than those of some speculative science, some speculative science is more certain in quantity. We hold the operable object, attainable by operation that is true praxis, to be most knowable in itself, so a science of it is exceeded by no other in quantity or proportion of certainty.
claims: All sciences are proportionally equally certain; they differ in quantity of certainty by their objects.
Theology's operable object, God, is most knowable, so its certainty is unsurpassed.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6766.summary: Reply to the argument from leisure: this science was not found for external necessities but internal ones, the moderation of passions and operations, as moral science would be no less practical if discovered when external needs were met. Nor was it found to escape ignorance, since much more knowable matter could have been included; rather the same things are repeated often to move the hearer more effectively to do what is urged.
claims: Theology addresses internal needs, the ordering of passions and acts.
Scripture's repetitions aim at moving to action, not at increasing knowledge.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6810.summary: Replies to the arguments of the second question. On De anima: Aristotle speaks of the end as known, since the intellect reasoning for something reasons for the end known as principle of demonstration.
claims: Aristotle's 'end' in De anima is the end as known, i.e. as principle.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6838.summary: On Metaphysics I: practical science is not for use as per se end, but has a relation to use such that use is its per se object, or something virtually including use, which for Aristotle is only a being for an end; every such object is less noble than a speculable one, so this ordering implies practical science's inferiority (on his premisses).
claims: Use is the object, not the end, of practical science.
For Aristotle practical objects are less noble than speculative ones.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6872.summary: On Metaphysics II: speculative and practical sciences have different per se ends within the genus of knowledge, but these do not distinguish them first; the prior distinction is by objects.
claims: Speculative and practical sciences differ first by objects, secondarily by ends.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6894.summary: Heading introducing replies to the arguments for the opposing opinion (practicality from the end).

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6904.summary: Reply to the first argument against distinction by objects: a speculative and a practical habit cannot concern the same object. Aristotle never said speculative intellect becomes practical by any extension. He posits three grades: considering speculables only; considering doables without dictating pursuit or avoidance; and, extending further, commanding pursuit or avoidance. The extension is from imperfectly to perfectly practical consideration, e.g. from apprehending fearsome things to a complete dictate commanding flight or pursuit.
claims: Speculative and practical habits cannot share an object.
Aristotle's 'extension' is from imperfectly to perfectly practical consideration.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6961.summary: Even granting that speculative intellect becomes practical by extension, it is irrelevant: speculative and practical are accidental differences of the intellect but essential ones of habits and acts, so habits and acts are not 'extended'.
claims: Practical and speculative are accidental to the intellect but essential to habits and acts.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e6981.summary: On medicine, someone says the universal habit is speculative but becomes practical when a particular habit is acquired from it. Against: then a practical conclusion would follow from speculative principles.
claims: Practical conclusions cannot follow from speculative principles.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e7002.summary: Scotus's reply: between opposite extremes, the further from one, the nearer the other. The most actually practical consideration is immediately and formally conformable to the praxis to be elicited; the further from this, the nearer the speculative. So a universal habit not immediately conformable can be called speculative relative to one that is, as art is relative to the expert's habit (the artisan often errs, the expert less). Thus medicine is divided into speculative (about universal causes and cures, remoter from praxis) and practical (about particulars). Yet in truth the more universal is simply practical, since it virtually includes the particular habit formally conformable to praxis.
claims: Practicality comes in degrees by proximity to praxis.
Universal practical knowledge is called speculative only relatively; it is simply practical.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e7094.summary: Reply to the argument from moral goodness: not every good act is first good from the circumstance of the end; some are good from the object, e.g. where the end is the object, so the end as object first gives rectitude. Loving God is simply good from its object alone without other circumstances. So it is false that moral goodness is first taken from the end as end as distinct from object; also false secondly, since even acts about means, though having the end as a circumstance, have a prior goodness from the object by which they are good in kind.
claims: Some acts, like loving God, are good from their object alone.
Generic goodness from the object is prior to goodness from the end.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e7144.summary: A third reply goes directly to the point: although a circumstance formally qualifies the praxis to make it good, it does not formally qualify the practical intellection. The intellect does not dictate moderately, as if its dictating were qualified by a mean; it dictates to the utmost of its power. Its dictate is right from a principle, and the principle is taken from the first object.
claims: Moral circumstances qualify praxis, not practical intellection.
The intellect's dictate is right from a principle derived from the first object.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e7181.summary: Objection to distinction by objects: whatever is formally such is so by something intrinsic; if a habit is formally practical, it is so by something intrinsic, which is not the object. As the sun is not formally hot though virtually hot.
claims: Formal practicality requires an intrinsic ground, which the object is not.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e7207.summary: Objection: the object distinguishes a habit only as efficient cause, and efficient causes do not distinguish effects in species, since specifically diverse causes can produce the same effect, as heat is produced univocally by fire and equivocally by the sun.
claims: Efficient causes do not specifically distinguish their effects.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e7231.summary: Reply to the first: being practical names something intrinsic to the knowledge, as an aptitudinal relation is intrinsic to its foundation; that some knowledge is apt to be so related is through its intrinsic nature, which it has from the object as extrinsic cause. So a habit is practical by something intrinsic as formal cause and by the object as efficient cause.
claims: A habit is practical formally by its intrinsic nature and efficiently by its object.

jdso8u-d1e167-d1e7265.summary: Reply to the second: from essentially ordered causes, one univocal and one equivocal, an effect of one ratio can come, as with heat. But when proximate efficient causes of the same order cause as distinct, especially if each is univocal with the effect, completely (likeness in form and mode of being) or diminishedly (likeness in form with another mode of being, like a house from the house in the mind), they cannot produce effects of one ratio. The object is the proximate, diminishedly univocal cause of knowledge, so formally distinct objects necessarily yield formally distinct knowledges.
claims: Distinct proximate univocal causes produce distinct effects.
The object is a proximate, diminishedly univocal cause of knowledge.
So formal distinction of objects entails formal distinction of knowledge.

jdso8u-d1e167.summary: Ordinatio I, Prologue part 5, two questions combined (Wadding q.4 and its companion): whether theology is practical, and whether a science is practical per se from its ordering to praxis as end. Scotus first defines praxis as an act of a power other than intellect, naturally posterior to intellection, apt to be elicited in conformity with right reason; hence primarily the elicited act of will, even without any commanded outward act. Practical knowledge extends to praxis by aptitudinal relations of conformity and natural priority, and is practical from its object, not from the end as end; he rejects Henry of Ghent's account of practical intellect and the view that practicality comes from the end. Against five ways holding theology speculative, affective or contemplative, and against views making it both speculative and practical (as two habits or one), he argues that all necessary theology in a created intellect is practical: its first subject, God as this essence, virtually contains the principles of right love, and even Trinitarian truths govern the rectitude of love of God. The love of the end is free and can be right or wrong, so knowledge directing it is practical, contrary to Aristotle, whose premiss of naturally necessary love the theologian rejects. Theology of contingents is not per se practical, since contingent rectitude (e.g. of eucharistic worship) is determined by the divine will, but it is accidentally practical for creatures. Whether God's own theology is practical is debated; Scotus inclines to say not, since the divine will is wholly its own rule. Replies show faith and the beatific vision are practical (ordered to enjoyment), that there is science of necessary truths about contingent acts, that practical knowledge of the end is the noblest, and that formally distinct objects cause formally distinct habits.
claims: Praxis is primarily the elicited act of will conformable to right reason.
Knowledge is practical by aptitudinal conformity and natural priority to right volition, grounded in its object, not its end.
All necessary theology in a created intellect is practical.
Love of the end is free praxis, so knowledge directing it is practical.
Theology of contingents is per se speculative but accidentally practical for creatures.
God's own theology is probably not practical, since the divine will is its own rule.
Practical knowledge about the ultimate end is nobler than any speculative knowledge.
